title: Distinct AI roles, one moderator
statement: Give each AI voice in a multi-voice discussion a distinct role and put one moderator in charge of turn order, since extra voices helped only once their roles differed.
example: Removing the AI classmates from one moderated classroom system cut student participation by a reported 26.5% and 45.2% on two engagement measures.
detail: Notes on a proposed discussion with several AI voices found that distinct agent roles beat a single generic agent or an undifferentiated panel: earlier multi-agent work found more agents helped only once roles differed, and a 2025 small RCT again found role identity, not agent count, drove the effect (`g9/library/collections/g3-repo-initiative-g9-othello-2026-10-01/research/idea-02-ai-classmates-multi-agent-debate.md`, lines 15-23). In an LLM classroom of teacher, assistant and classmate agents tested online with 400+ students, removing the classmates cut participation by a reported 26.5% and 45.2% on two engagement metrics, in a system that also has a moderator governing turn order so classmates don't crowd the student out (lines 34-39). The project's synthesis concluded that gains come from distinct roles plus a moderator, not from more voices (`g9/library/collections/g3-repo-initiative-g9-othello-2026-10-01/research/IDEA-SYNTHESIS.md`, line 16).
against: The moderator half is a design inference: the ablation removed the classmate agents, not the moderator, and the notes tag the result as a field study and ablation in a preprint, not independently replicated (`g9/library/collections/g3-repo-initiative-g9-othello-2026-10-01/research/idea-02-ai-classmates-multi-agent-debate.md`, lines 36-39). No study tests a live, voice-based debate among several AI voices about literature with learners aged 13 to 18 directly (the same file, line 146).

evidence.quote: **1. Distinct agent *roles* beat a single generic agent or an undifferentiated panel.**
A 2025 ACM study retesting this with modern conversational agents again finds role identity, not agent count, drives the effect **(small RCT)**.
Earlier multi-agent work ("Togetherness," 2014) found *more* agents helped only once roles differed — extra undifferentiated voices did not reproduce the gain **(small observational study)**.

Removing the classmate agents cut student participation substantially (reported 26.5%/45.2% drops on two engagement metrics) — but the system also has an explicit "class control mechanism" (a moderator governing turn order) so classmates don't crowd the student out
Gains come from **distinct roles plus a moderator**, not from more voices
